summary: This OECD Taxing Wages 2019 annex explains the methodology and limitations behind the report's comparative tax, benefit and labour cost statistics across OECD countries. It defines eight household types built around an average full-time worker earning a fraction of average wages, and details the earnings data sources, industry coverage (ISIC Sectors B-N, later ISIC Rev. 4), 2018 wage estimation method, exchange rates and PPPs, and what taxes and benefits are covered. The note is partly truncated at the end, cutting off mid-discussion of standard tax reliefs.
one_line: OECD annex describing the methodology, household types, earnings data and limitations behind the Taxing Wages 2019 comparative tax statistics.
key_facts: The Taxing Wages 2019 report focuses on eight household types that vary by composition and level of earnings.
Each household contains a full-time adult employee, and the annual income from employment is assumed to be a given fraction of average gross wage earnings.
Any children in the household are assumed to be aged between six and eleven inclusive.
The standard assumption for calculating average wage earnings is based on Sectors B-N of ISIC Revision 4 (United Nations).
The 2005 edition of Taxing Wages used sectors C-K incl. of ISIC Revision 3.1.
Chile, Ireland, Slovak Republic and Turkey cannot exclude or convert part-time workers' wages, so their reported average wages will be lower than an average of full-time workers.
An OECD Secretariat analysis found full-time employees' earnings in 2014 were on average 12% higher than earnings of all employees in selected European countries.
Excluding supervisory and management employees can reduce average earnings by 10% to 18%, according to an OECD Secretariat analysis of Eurostat data.
Fringe benefits rarely account for more than 1-2% of labour costs and are excluded where possible from average earnings.
In the United States, employers' contributions to private pension, family allowance or health and life insurance schemes can account for more than 5% of employee earnings and are excluded.

Statistical data on average gross wage earnings in 2018 were generally not available, so 2018 estimates were derived by multiplying 2017 earnings by the country-specific annual percentage change of wages in the OECD Economic Outlook.
Thirteen OECD member countries provided national estimates of 2018 average gross wage earnings, which were not used in the Taxing Wages calculations except for listed countries.

Treaty-free coverage includes personal income tax, employee and employer social security contributions, and payroll taxes, while income tax on capital income, net wealth tax, corporate income tax and all indirect taxes are not considered.
Compulsory social security contributions paid to general government are treated as tax revenues in the Report.
The 2018 exchange rate for the United States is 1.00 USD, and the 2018 PPP for the United Kingdom is 0.69 GBP.

entities.role: country whose part-time worker wages cannot be excluded from its average wage figures
